page: Amazon Web Services r7iz.metal-16xl is a bare-metal, memory-optimized server powered by dedicated Intel Xeon 6455B processors. It features 64 vCPUs across 32 physical cores with hyper-threading, operating at a clock speed of 3.9 GHz and supported by a 60 MB L3 cache. The system is equipped with 512.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory running at 5 GHz, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per core. It lacks local storage and dedicated GPU hardware, relying instead on network-attached storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 25 Gbps.

In benchmark testing, the r7iz.metal-16xl demonstrates strong processing and memory capabilities. It achieves top-tier status in Geekbench single-core (2285.0) and multi-core (22751.0) scores, placing it in the top 10% of tested systems. The processor's advanced instruction sets, including Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) and AVX-512, contribute to strong Passmark CPU extended instructions performance (89076.49) and efficient LLM inference, processing 297.6 tokens per second on a medium 7B model. Memory performance is robust, with cached read-only small block bandwidth reaching 5705.78 GB/sec and uncached large block read bandwidth at 244.66 GB/sec.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, this bare-metal instance offers high resource density and memory performance for enterprise workloads without the overhead of a hypervisor. However, the absence of local NVMe SSDs and dedicated GPUs represents a clear tradeoff, making it dependent on network storage for data persistence and less suitable for heavy graphics or GPU-bound machine learning training. The server is highly optimized for memory-intensive and compute-heavy applications, such as large-scale in-memory databases, software compilation, and CPU-based AI inference.

The instance delivers top-tier performance, scoring in the top 10% for Geekbench single-core (2285.0) and multi-core (22751.0) benchmarks, alongside strong memory bandwidth of 244.66 GB/sec for uncached large blocks. This server is highly efficient for memory-intensive enterprise workloads, including in-memory databases, Redis deployments, and CPU-based machine learning inference, where hypervisor overhead must be avoided.
